opus-5.5.text:
You have to remember what the environment was like back then. This was around 2007. Today, if an undergraduate in China has a CVPR paper, people still think it's impressive but not shocking. There are labs everywhere, senior students mentor you, and you can download code from GitHub and build on it. Back then there was almost none of that.

At a mainland Chinese university, very few people were publishing at top international venues at all, even among faculty and PhD students. CVPR felt like something happening in another world, at Berkeley, MIT, CMU, or maybe Microsoft Research Asia. For an undergraduate to walk into that world with a first-author paper was almost unheard of.

What made it more remarkable was the kind of paper it was. His spectral residual work on saliency detection wasn't an incremental tweak on someone else's system. It was a simple, elegant idea: look at the log spectrum of an image, find what deviates from the statistical regularity, and treat that as what's "salient." It was a few lines of code, it worked surprisingly well, and it got cited a lot. That's the kind of paper that comes from real intuition, not from having a lot of resources.

For people like me at Jiao Tong a few years later, he was proof that it was possible. You didn't have to wait until you went abroad for a PhD to do research that the international community would take seriously. I think that example mattered a lot, maybe more than the paper itself. It changed what students around us believed they were allowed to aim for.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts today’s impressive but more common undergraduate CVPR papers with the period around 2007, when few people at mainland Chinese universities published at top international venues and an undergraduate first-author CVPR paper was almost unheard of.

fable-5.1.text:
You have to remember what the landscape looked like back then. Around 2007, 2008, computer vision in mainland China was really in its infancy. CVPR was the top venue, and the papers there came overwhelmingly from the US and Europe, from groups like MIT, Berkeley, Oxford, CMU. If a Chinese institution showed up, it was usually MSRA, which was essentially a foreign lab planted in Beijing, or maybe a handful of professors who had come back from abroad. For a domestic university to get a paper in, with a student as first author, was already rare. For that student to be an undergraduate was almost unheard of.

And it wasn't just that he got in. The saliency paper was genuinely influential. It was a very simple idea, spectral residual, you could implement it in a few lines of MATLAB, and people actually used it and built on it for years. It became one of those baseline methods everyone cites. So this wasn't a case of someone squeezing through with a marginal paper. He had an original insight, he figured out how to communicate it in the form the international community expected, and he did all of that basically on his own, without the kind of mentorship pipeline that students at Stanford or MIT took for granted.

For those of us who were undergraduates in China at the same time, that was a huge psychological thing. We were reading these papers and treating the authors as almost mythical figures. Then suddenly here is someone from Shanghai Jiao Tong, our age, doing it. It made the whole thing feel reachable. I think a lot of people from my generation who ended up going into vision research can point to that moment, not just Xiaodi specifically, but that realization that the gap was not as large as we had imagined. He was really one of the first to prove it.

r001.rationale: The response says an undergraduate CVPR publication from a mainland Chinese university was almost unheard of around 2007–08, but it does not compare that rarity with the situation for undergraduates today.

astra-6.text: You have to put it in the context of that time. For an undergraduate at a mainland Chinese university, the path to publishing at CVPR wasn’t nearly as established. You needed not only a strong idea, but also the initiative to understand what the international research community cared about and how to contribute to it. Doing that so early made Xiaodi’s achievement stand out. It showed that an undergraduate could produce research that belonged on that stage.

r001.rationale: The response says the path to CVPR publication was less established at the time, but does not clearly compare how exceptional it was then with undergraduates today.

Today, undergraduates publishing at CVPR is much more common, but back then, for someone at a mainland Chinese university, it was extraordinary. There weren’t established pipelines where you could join a lab, get a well-defined project, and receive detailed guidance on how to publish at a top conference. Even knowing what problems the international community cared about was a barrier. So what impressed me about Xiaodi was the independence that achievement represented: as an undergraduate, he could identify an interesting problem and produce work that the international community recognized. For students like me, that made a very strong impression.
